task_row_model.query: Let p(x) be a cubic polynomial. Given p(1)=4, p(2)=7, p(4)=19, and p(5)=28, determine p(0).

documents.content: Textbook excerpt — algebraic interpolation. A polynomial of degree at most three is uniquely determined by its values at four distinct abscissas. The Newton divided-difference form constructs p(x)=a0 + a1(x-x0)+a2(x-x0)(x-x1)+a3(x-x0)(x-x1)(x-x2) from four data points; evaluating that form at x=0 yields p(0). In practice one computes successive divided differences from the given y-values to obtain coefficients a0..a3. Historically, finite-difference and Newton forms were favored for hand computation because they reuse previously computed differences, though we omit further historical detail here.

Problem report — contest example. Consider the cubic polynomial p(x) used in an olympiad-style exercise: p(1)=4, p(2)=7, p(4)=19, p(5)=28. The statement supplies four explicit point-values but does not list coefficients. Solvers commonly record the given pairs (1,4), (2,7), (4,19), (5,28) and set up an interpolation system or use finite differences. The short problem statement emphasizes those four numerical constraints and asks for p evaluated at another integer, typically p(0) or p(3), to exploit integral-pattern structure in the values.

Informal note by an instructor. Let p(x) be a cubic polynomial with integer coefficients; many classroom exercises pick integer coefficients so outputs at integer inputs are integers. Given that assumption, any reconstructed p will have integer values at integer x, so p(0) will be an integer. One can use forward differences or solve the 4×4 linear system for coefficients; sometimes one looks for patterns in consecutive differences to reduce algebra. There is also speculative commentary among students about guessing low-magnitude integer coefficients, but such guesses must be verified algebraically.

Reference entry — interpolation overview and historical tangents. Lagrange interpolation provides an explicit polynomial formula as a sum of basis polynomials L_j(x) multiplied by given y_j, often illustrated with degree-two examples in classical texts. The entry digresses into the 19th-century history of numerical tables, cites adoption in early engineering, and lists unrelated statistics about table compilation times. It also restates the general theorem that n+1 data points determine a degree-n polynomial, then discusses computational complexity and ties to spline methods—material adjacent but not required for elementary pointwise reconstruction.

task_row_model.golden_answer: p is a cubic polynomial (degree 3) with integer coefficients. Its given values are p(1)=4, p(2)=7, p(4)=19, and p(5)=28. Four values at distinct x determine a unique cubic polynomial, so these constraints suffice to compute p(0); with integer coefficients, the resulting p(0) is an integer.
